content: Plasmodium malariae is a parasitic protozoan responsible for causing malaria in both humans and dogs. It is closely related to Plasmodium falciparum and Plasmodium vivax, which are the primary causative agents of most malarial infections. However, P. malariae is often referred to as causing benign malaria, as it is significantly less dangerous compared to the infections caused by P. falciparum or P. vivax. The fevers associated with P. malariae occur at approximately three-day intervals, a pattern known as quartan fever. This interval is longer than the two-day cycles typically seen with other malarial parasites. Microscopically, red blood cells (erythrocytes) infected by P. malariae are not enlarged and may even appear smaller than normal red blood cells. The cytoplasm of the infected cells remains intact without decolorization, and no dots are visible on the cell surface. The parasite itself is compact, with a small food vacuole. It is uncommon for a single red blood cell to host more than one parasite. A distinctive feature of P. malariae is the presence of band forms, where the parasite forms a thick band across the width of the infected red blood cell. This characteristic is often considered diagnostic of this species. Additionally, large grains of malarial pigment are frequently observed in P. malariae infections, more so than in any other Plasmodium species. It is important to note that blood samples containing P. vivax or P. ovale that have been sitting in EDTA for more than 30 minutes before the preparation of a blood film may appear very similar to P. malariae under the microscope. This similarity underscores the critical need to alert the laboratory immediately when a blood sample is drawn, ensuring that the sample is processed as quickly as possible to avoid diagnostic confusion.
